blocks.text: [III, 190] III. The third passage is Es. XIV, 29. (var. XV, 2.): Rejoice not, thou whole Palestine, because the rod of him that smote thee is broken. For out of the serpent's root shall come forth צפע, a basilisk. King Uzziah (under whom Isaiah had been called by God to the prophetic office, [col. 405] Es. I, 1.) had for a time harassed the Philistines with a heavy war, pulling down the walls of Gath, Jabneh and Ashdod, and building cities in the middle of Philistia, 2 Paral. XXVI, 6. But when he tried to usurp the priestly office, he was deposed from the kingship and died in a separate house. He was succeeded by Jotham and Ahaz. Under Ahaz the Philistines recovered their courage and strength, invaded the lowland and southern towns of Judah, took Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Socho, Timnah and Gimzo with the neighbouring villages, and settled there. For the Lord had brought the Jews low because of the impiety of Ahaz, 2 Par. XXVIII, 18. 19. But in the very year in which Ahaz died (Es. XIV, 28.), Isaiah, full of God, foretells a great change of affairs soon to come under Ahaz's successor Hezekiah, who subdued the Philistines as far as Gaza, 2 Reg. XVIII, 8. Accordingly the holy Prophet says here, Rejoice not, thou whole Palestine, because the rod of him that smote thee is broken; that is: All you Philistines, who once exulted at the deposition and death of King Uzziah, who had treated you harshly, and who under Ahaz dared to rise against our people, rejoice no longer. For out of the serpent's root, that is, out of the stock of Uzziah, who had stung you like a serpent, comes forth another serpent, namely Hezekiah, and he one of the most deadly kind, a basilisk, whom you will find more grievous and more hostile than Uzziah himself, to your very great harm. Hence Jerome on this passage: Rejoice not, O Philistia, do not insult my people, etc., because the staff that was wont to strike thee seems broken by death, because the snake is slain. For in his place a more harmful one shall be born, Hezekiah, a regulus, which the Greeks call basilisk, which shall kill thee with its look and slay thee with the breath of its mouth. For as no bird can pass the regulus's sight unharmed, but, however far off it be, is swallowed by its mouth, so thou too shalt wholly perish at the sight of King Hezekiah. And he has kept the metaphor finely; for since he had named a serpent and a regulus, he says that birds are devoured by its mouth and breath. For in Jerome's version the whole verse we are treating reads thus: For out of the root of the snake shall come forth a regulus, and its seed swallowing the bird. The holy man applies its last words to the story of the basilisk, of which Solinus says: It corrupts even the air itself, so that no bird flies across the air with impunity, since it is infected with its pestilent breath. And from him Isidore: At its sight no flying bird passes unharmed, but, however far off it may be, it is burnt and devoured by its mouth. And Avicenna: انّ حاني مسكنها طاير سقط [inna ḥānī maskanihā ṭāyir saqaṭa] A bird falls whenever it is over against its lair. And Alkazuinius: ان طار طاير فوقها سقط عليها [in ṭāra ṭāyir fawqahā saqaṭa ʿalayhā] If a bird flies over it, it falls upon it. So also Damir. But these things are not very certain, nor, as far as I remember, were they reported by anyone before Solinus, who is not the best of authors. [III, 191] And Isaiah is cited in vain, since the Hebrew reads, as Jerome himself acknowledges in his Notes, ופריו שרף מעופף, And its fruit a flying serpent (or rather hydrus), which will be explained below. Whoever therefore first rendered those words And its seed swallowing the bird read שואף, which means swallowing, instead of שרף. But truly there is no need here to search laboriously for reasons why King Hezekiah is compared to a serpent or a basilisk, since it is nothing new for a powerful king to be represented by a serpent. So among the Egyptians, who were neighbours of the Philistines, as Aelian writes in History, book 6, chapter 38: Τοὺς βασιλεῖς ἐπὶ τῶν διαδημάτων φορεῖν πεποικιλμένας ἀσπίδας, τῆς ἀρχῆς αἰνιττομένους τὸ ἀνίκητον [Tous basileis epi tōn diadēmatōn phorein pepoikilmenas aspidas, tēs archēs ainittomenous to anikēton], The kings wore painted asps on their diadems, to signify the invincible power of their rule. Namely because τῶν ὑπ᾽ ἀσπίδος δηχθέντων οὐ μνημονεύεται οὐδεὶς ἐξάντης γεγονέναι τοῦ κακοῦ [tōn hyp᾽ aspidos dēchthentōn ou mnēmoneuetai oudeis exantēs gegonenai tou kakou], of those bitten by an asp, no one is ever recorded to have escaped. And Horus, book 1, [col. 406] chapter 56: Βασιλέα δὲ κάκισον (read κράτισον) δηλοῦντες, ὄφιν ζωγραφοῦσι κοσμοειδῶς ἐσχηματισμένον, οὗ τὴν οὐρὰν ἐν τῷ στόματι ποιοῦσι· [Basilea de kakison (read kratison) dēlountes, ophin zōgraphousi kosmoeidōs eschēmatismenon, hou tēn ouran en tō stomati poiousi] To signify a most powerful king, they paint a serpent with its tail in its mouth in the shape of a circle: namely to indicate that he rules the whole circle of the earth. Read also chapters 57, 58 and 61, in all of which various virtues or duties of kings are signified by a serpent, whether watchful, or coiled, or half, or whole. But among all kinds of serpents the basilisk above all is the figure of a king. For this is signified by the Arabic name ملكة [malika] melecha, the Greek βασιλίσκου [basiliskou] and the Latin REGULUS. Thus Nicander, Theriaca line 397, calls it ἑρπηςῶν βασιλῆα [herpēstōn basilēa], king of reptiles. And Pliny describes it as marked by a white spot on the head, as if by a kind of diadem. And Solinus: its head lined with white as if with a little mitre. Galen too, and Aëtius: θηρίον ἐπὶ τῇ κεφαλῇ τρεῖς ὑπεροχὰς ἔχον [thērion epi tē kephalē treis hyperochas echon], a serpent having three prominences on its head. And Avicenna: مكللة الراس [mukallalat al-rās] with crowned head. And Damir: علي راسه خطوط بيض مثل التاج [ʿalī rāsihi khuṭūṭ bīḍ mithl al-tāj] having white lines on its head like a crown. And Alkazuinius: قال جالينوس انها حية شقرا علي راسها ثلاث قنازع مثل التاج [qāla Jālīnūs innahā ḥayya shaqrā ʿalī rāsihā thalāth qanāziʿ mithl al-tāj] Galen said that it is a reddish snake, and has on its head three crests in the manner of a crown ^{(5)}. They add that it does not, like the others, crawl prone with its whole body, [III, 192] but with its head and the middle part of its body raised. Pliny: It does not drive its body forward with manifold coiling, like the other serpents, but advances lofty and erect in the middle. Solinus: When it moves, it crawls with the middle part of its body, while the other half is raised and lofty. As if this were the badge of royalty, as for the kings of the Persians to wear τὴν τιάραν ὀρθὴν [tēn tiaran orthēn] [the upright tiara]. Moreover, every kind of reptile gives way to it, however small, as if acknowledging it as king; for it puts them to flight with its hiss, as we have shown above ^{c)},
